text: I have read both inputs and am checking a source-identity mismatch before developing a connection: inputs/Q.tex is Garjani et al., “A Systematic Approach to Mechanism Design with Stochastic Dynamic Stability,” whereas inputs/P.tex cites a different Q (Struski et al. on LLM double auctions) and a different P (Hansen et al. on token energy). I will treat the actual input texts as the pair, verify Q’s theorems and P’s status, then assess whether any supported cross-paper advance survives.

Input mismatch to flag before transfer: actual Q (inputs/Q.tex, abstract; Sections 2–4) is Garjani et al. on strongly concave separable stochastic resource allocation and quadratic LMI transfers. Actual P (inputs/P.tex, Setting and contribution) is a proposal for token charges in a fixed-value LLM double auction, but its own text calls Struski et al. auction paper “Q” and Hansen et al. energy paper “P.” Those labels do not describe the assigned Q/P pair. I am testing a narrower bridge: Q allocates scarce resources; P makes inference tokens a measurable scarce resource. Need check whether auction spillovers defeat Q’s separable-valuation assumption.

For the actual Q–P pairing, the useful bridge is costly computation versus Q’s budget balance/individual rationality. Q defines \(U_n=V_n(x_n)-t_n\) and proves only \(U_n(s^*)\geq V_n(0)=0\) (Problem Formulation P3–P4; Proposition IR_prop); P defines cost-aware welfare \(W_\lambda=G-\lambda C\) and explicitly prices each generated-token decision (Gross and net surplus; Mechanism and test). If Q’s learning makes agent \(n\) pay real cost \(c_n>0\), ex ante payoff is \(V_n(x_n^*)-t_n(s^*)-c_n\); Q’s IR theorem no longer guarantees participation. With balanced transfers, summing ex ante IR gives necessary condition \(\sum_n V_n(x_n^*)\geq\sum_n c_n\). The open research question is whether one can preserve Q’s implementation/stability while internalizing metered learning costs and retaining budget balance plus ex ante IR. P does not test Q’s mechanism or establish an effect.

A necessary feasibility bound combines actual Q's P3/P4 (inputs/Q.tex, mechanism goals around lines 169–178: \(\sum_i t_i=0\), \(U_i\geq0\)) with actual P's accounting (inputs/P.tex, Gross and net surplus: \(G^{\star}=7.5\) per round and \(W_{\lambda}=G-\lambda C\)). If traders' outside payoffs are zero and token expenditure is a real external cost, summing \(U_i=g_i-\lambda c_i-t_i\) gives \(\sum_i U_i=G-\lambda C\leq7.5-\lambda C\). Thus \(\lambda C>7.5\) rules out simultaneous budget balance and individual rationality for that round, regardless of the payment rule. At the accounting level \(G\geq\lambda C\) also suffices for some unrestricted lump-sum redistribution, but not for Nash implementation or private-information incentives. This is a sharper Q/P bridge than transplanting Q's tax directly.

Q-specific counterexample to cost-blind IR: take \(N=2,K=1,\mathcal X_1=\mathcal X_2=[0,1],c=2\), \(V_1(x)=-x^2/2\), \(V_2(x)=x-x^2/2\). These satisfy Q’s convex/compact and strongly concave valuation assumptions with \(V_n(0)=0\). The welfare optimum is \(x^*=(0,1)\) with slack capacity and shadow price \(\lambda^o=0\); in Q’s explicit payment (eq. (40)), \(p^*=0\) makes every \(t_n=0\). Thus Q’s ex post IR holds tightly for agent 1: \(U_1=0\). Any mandatory first decision costing \(c_1>0\), as P’s proposed charge counts (Mechanism and test), gives ex ante payoff \(-c_1<0\). This is a counterexample to carrying Q’s IR guarantee over to metered learning, not a counterexample to Q’s original theorem. I sharpen the broad pair question to finite-cost learning with budget balance and ex ante IR.

Distinct conditional no-go from Q Theorem 4 + P cost accounting: Q sets \(Q_i=\lceil C_b/\eta^{2(i+1)}\rceil\) with \(0<\eta<1\) (inputs/Q.tex, Theorem 4, lines 518–520), so \(\sum_{i=0}^{I-1}Q_i\to\infty\), indeed geometrically. Q's \(V_n\) are continuous on compact \(\mathcal X_n\) (Assumptions 1–2), giving finite \(M=\max_x\sum_nV_n(x_n)\). If the valuation samples in this algorithm are implemented by token-generating calls costing at least \(d>0\) per sample, and the value is realized once after learning, cumulative real cost is at least \(dN\sum_{i<I}Q_i\). With no external subsidy and total transfers balanced, summed ex ante payoff is at most \(M-dN\sum_{i<I}Q_i\), eventually negative; hence universal ex ante IR cannot persist along Q's infinite-sample convergence schedule. This does not criticize Q's original setting: its random samples need not be LLM calls, and Q's IR theorem concerns equilibrium payoff after learning, not paid training. It motivates a finite-accuracy, cost-aware stopping/learning mechanism. P (Gross and net surplus; Mechanism and test) supplies the token metering motivation, not a theorem that Q's oracle uses tokens.

A second concrete constraint from Q’s own learning theorem: Q Theorem 4 sets \(Q_i=\lceil C_b/\eta^{2(i+1)}\rceil\) with \(0<\eta<1\), so \(\sum_{i=0}^{I-1}Q_i\geq C_b\sum_{i=0}^{I-1}\eta^{-2(i+1)}\to\infty\). If one stochastic-sample evaluation has positive metered cost, every finite agent budget (as in P’s finite-budget arm and its description of energy exhaustion) stops Q’s algorithm after finitely many iterations; Q’s asymptotic mean-square conclusion is then not a finite-budget guarantee. This is conditional on sample evaluations being charged; P meters LLM tokens, while Q’s samples need not be LLM calls. Q Numerical Simulations also says \(Q_i=\lceil\tilde\eta^{i+1}\rceil\) with \(\tilde\eta=0.96\), which equals \(1\) at every iteration and differs from Theorem 4’s growing schedule. That discrepancy needs checking before using Q’s plots as finite-budget evidence.

Obstruction to a direct Q-tax transplant into P's auction: Q's planner objective is \(\sum_n V_n(x_n)\) with each \(V_n\) depending only on agent \(n\)'s continuous convex-set allocation, and strong concavity is Assumption 2 (inputs/Q.tex, Problem Formulation). P's gross surplus is computed from executed buyer–seller matches (inputs/P.tex, Gross and net surplus). Even a one-buyer, one-seller example with trade surplus \(h>0\) and one required call each has \(G(x_b,x_s)=h x_bx_s\) for binary participation; the cross-difference is \(h\), whereas every additive \(V_b(x_b)+V_s(x_s)\) has zero cross-difference. Binary calls also violate Q's convex allocation sets. A convex surrogate with fixed counterpart response would be an additional model, not an application of Q's theorem to P as written.

The impossibility/IR inequality alone is too elementary for a publication claim. Targeted prior-work search queries: “mechanism design costly computation agent budget balanced arxiv”, “mechanism design computation costs learning equilibrium participation arxiv”, and “site:arxiv.org \"budget balance\" \"computation cost\" \"individual rationality\"”. Adjacent primary work includes “Delegating Computation on Costly Data” (https://people.csail.mit.edu/silvio/Selected%20Scientific%20Papers/Mechanism%20Design/Delegating%20Computation%20On%20Costly%20Data.pdf) and “Bayesian Mechanism Design for Budget-Constrained Agents” (https://arxiv.org/abs/1103.6280), though neither search result settles this exact Q/P question. A publishable contribution would need a finite-budget learning/transfer construction with quantitative efficiency and ex ante IR guarantees, or a stronger impossibility under Q’s information constraints. No novelty claim from this search.

Scope refinement: if Q fixes every agent’s sample count \(Q_i\) and metered cost is independent of that agent’s messages, subtracting the already-incurred cost from stage utility does not change Q’s best-response equations or the Nash allocation. It changes the ex ante participation decision. Behavioural effects analogous to P’s charged quote decisions require endogenous choices (whether to join/withdraw, how many samples or tokens to buy, or whether to continue learning). The proposed research target should therefore be finite-horizon, endogenous sampling/entry with private or heterogeneous costs; simply adding a constant cost to Q’s stage game is not a new mechanism result.

I wrote the derivation and precise scope in emmy/costly_learning_note.tex. It proves the accounting feasibility condition \(G\geq\lambda C\) for balanced transfers plus zero-baseline IR, the conditional finite-iteration bound for Q's Theorem 4 when each sample has positive token cost, and the buyer–seller complementarity obstruction to directly applying Q's separable-valuation theorem to P's auction. Style bans and style gate pass; the TeX compiles to a three-page PDF in temporary storage. This is a candidate research question about finite-cost learning with ex ante IR, not a claim that Q's original theorem is false.

Quantitative finite-cost cap (conditional): let \(M=\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\sum_nV_n(x_n)<\infty\) from Q’s compactness/continuity, let each sample cost at least \(d>0\), and suppose one allocation payoff is realized after \(I\) rounds of Q’s Theorem 4 schedule. Then \(dN\sum_{i=0}^{I-1}Q_i\geq dNC_b(\eta^{-2I}-1)/(1-\eta^2)\). Balanced transfers plus ex ante IR require nonnegative net total, hence necessarily \(I\leq \log(1+M(1-\eta^2)/(dNC_b))/(2\log(1/\eta))\) when \(M\geq0\). This is a finite iteration ceiling for any such implementation; it does not imply a performance guarantee at that stopping point. It sharpens the new question: find a finite-budget policy with an explicit welfare/accuracy guarantee and cost-sharing rule, or prove none under Q’s local-information constraints.

Independent prior-work check narrows novelty: targeted queries were “budget balanced mechanism costly information acquisition endogenous sampling equilibrium learning participation research paper”, “mechanism design costly computation stochastic optimization sample acquisition budget balance individual rationality”, and “learning in games costly observations budget balanced transfers mechanism design finite sample”. Osborne, Rosenthal, and Stewart, Information Aggregation with Costly Reporting (https://academic.oup.com/ej/article/130/625/208/5593948), already studies costly signal disclosure and shows transfers between individuals can restore first-best decisions in its model. Chen et al., Optimal Data Acquisition for Statistical Estimation (https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/dxhp4-jvk64), already designs an IR, incentive-compatible budget-constrained data-acquisition mechanism. Therefore general metered learning, balanced transfers, and IR are not new. The plausible open target, if any, is a finite-budget, endogenous-sampling/stopping extension of Q's specific stochastic NE implementation with explicit oracle costs, or a rigorous impossibility under its information and balance constraints. These queries and two adjacent papers do not establish novelty.

Cross-check of the counterexample against Q’s exact eq. (40): at \(N=2,c=2,p_{-n}=0\), each deviator’s tax is \(t_n=\alpha[p_n^2/2+p_n(2-x_n-x_{-n})]\geq0\) for \(x_n,x_{-n}\in[0,1]\). Thus \((x_1,x_2,p_1,p_2)=(0,1,0,0)\) is genuinely a Nash profile: each valuation is maximized at the stated own allocation and no positive price reduces tax. With \(c_1=0.1,c_2=0\), total net value remains \(0.5-0.1=0.4>0\), yet agent 1’s ex ante payoff under Q’s tax is \(-0.1\). This separates aggregate feasibility from failure of Q’s particular transfer to compensate a participant with zero gross benefit.

A sharper type-space counterexample than waiting for Q's growing schedule: choose \(\mathcal X_n=[0,1]\) and \(V_n(x_n)=-\alpha x_n^2/2\) for every agent, with any nonnegative capacity. These satisfy Q's compactness, smoothness, strong concavity, and \(V_n(0)=0\); welfare optimum has \(G=0\). If every entrant must pay for even one token-generating sample before opting out, then \(C>0\). For any balanced transfers, \(\sum_n u_n=G-\lambda C<0\), so universal ex ante IR fails for at least one agent. Therefore a paid-oracle extension over Q's full valuation class must allow costless pre-sample opt-out, an external subsidy, or a restricted type class with guaranteed gains. This is conditional on samples being metered; it is not a flaw in Q's original post-learning IR theorem.

My best account is a conditional research lead, not a finished publication result. Actual Q’s Problem Formulation and IR proposition guarantee \(\sum t_n=0\) and \(V_n-t_n\geq0\) only at its ideal Nash equilibrium; its Theorem 4 uses a geometrically growing sample schedule. Actual P’s Gross and net surplus section makes costly decisions explicit via \(W_\lambda=G-\lambda C\), while Mechanism and test distinguishes a first charged decision, withdrawal, and finite-budget exhaustion. Together they expose the omitted ex ante participation and finite-resource problem. Q’s own eq. (40) has a concrete positive-net-surplus counterexample to cost-aware IR (entry 14), and the conditional finite-iteration cap is in entry 12. Directly treating P’s double auction as Q’s separable concave allocation violates Q’s assumptions (emmy entry 8). Remaining work for a paper: define endogenous sample/withdrawal decisions and cost observability, prove a finite-budget welfare/error plus budget-balance/ex ante-IR result or a stronger impossibility, and test it. The elementary accounting bound and search do not establish novelty; P contains no such experiment, and Q’s stochastic samples need not be LLM tokens.

Cross-check of emmy entry 15: accepted. With \(V_n(x)=-\alpha x^2/2\) on \([0,1]\), each function is strongly concave, smooth and normalized at zero as Q requires; \(x^*=0\) gives gross welfare \(0\). If a positive-cost first sample is mandatory for every entrant and transfers sum to zero, \(\sum_n(V_n(x_n^*)-t_n-c_n)=-\sum_n c_n<0\), so at least one agent cannot satisfy ex ante IR. This stronger full-type-space obstruction means a universal paid-learning extension needs a costless entry screen, external funding, or a restricted class with positive surplus. My positive-surplus example (entry 14) adds that even when redistribution is feasible in aggregate, Q’s particular eq. (40) does not supply it.

Current synthesis and sharpened question: For Q's separable, strongly concave stochastic resource-allocation game, suppose each agent can choose paid sample acquisitions or exit before further learning. Can a finite-budget mechanism preserve an explicit approximate-Nash/welfare guarantee together with ex ante IR and balanced transfers, or is that impossible under Q's local-information constraints? Q's equilibrium BB/IR and Theorem 4 (inputs/Q.tex, mechanism goals, IR proposition, Theorem 4) supply the structure and geometric-sampling baseline; P's Gross and net surplus and Mechanism and test (inputs/P.tex) supply metered-cost accounting and the entry/withdrawal distinction. Established here: \(G\geq\lambda C\) is necessary for BB+IR; a mandatory positive-cost first sample fails on Q's full type class; Q's exponential schedule has a finite-cost iteration cap when samples are token calls. Direct use of Q's tax for P's auction fails separability. The note emmy/costly_learning_note.tex now includes these limits and the fixed-cost best-response caveat. This is a supported research lead, not yet a publishable result; unresolved are the oracle-cost model, cost observability, endogenous sampling incentives, finite-error guarantee, and novelty relative to adjacent costly-information mechanisms.

Design consequence of the actual texts: Q, inputs/Q.tex, Individual rationality (P4), proves (U_n(s^*)\geq V_n(0)=0) by comparing with a zero-allocation deviation inside its stage game. P, inputs/P.tex, Mechanism and test, explicitly charges the first scheduled decision, including withdrawal. Under the mandatory paid-oracle bridge, that withdrawal is too late to serve as the costless entry screen needed for Q\(\text{ }\)s full valuation class (emmy #15). A viable ex ante-IR extension must allow opt-out before the first metered call, subsidize it, or restrict types to sufficient expected gain. This is a design constraint on a new mechanism, not an empirical claim about P\(\text{ }\)s auction.

TeX correction to #21: Q, inputs/Q.tex, Individual rationality (P4), proves \(U_n(s^*)\geq V_n(0)=0\) through a zero-allocation deviation within its stage game. P, inputs/P.tex, Mechanism and test, charges the first scheduled decision even when the trader withdraws. Under a mandatory paid-oracle extension of Q, that withdrawal occurs after the first cost and cannot be the costless entry screen needed over the full valuation class. A feasible ex ante-IR design needs opt-out before the first charged call, outside funding, or a restricted type class. The substantive conclusion in #21 is unchanged.

Cross-check of ada #21 against actual texts: Q, inputs/Q.tex, Individual rationality (P4) proof, uses the within-game deviation \(s_n^{\prime}=\operatorname{col}(0,\tilde p)\) and concludes \(U_n(s^*)\geq U_n(s_n^{\prime},s_{-n}^*)\geq0\). That comparison contains no reimbursement for an earlier paid learning call. P, inputs/P.tex, Mechanism and test, proposes a persistent withdrawal option but explicitly charges the first scheduled decision, including withdrawal. Hence withdrawal on that call is too late to be a costless pre-call entry screen under the conditional paid-oracle bridge. A pre-call opt-out, external subsidy, or restricted positive-gain type class is needed to evade the zero-gain counterexample in #15; a costless opt-out alone does not give a welfare guarantee. I added the timing distinction to emmy/costly_learning_note.tex; style checks pass and it compiles to three pages.
